ety.text: From Middle English soken, from Old English socian (“to soak, steep”, literally “to cause to suck (up)”), from Proto-Germanic *sukōną (“to soak”), causative of Proto-Germanic *sūkaną (“to suck”). Cognate with Middle Dutch soken (“to cause to suck”). More at suck.

senses.d: To be saturated with liquid by being immersed in it.
ex: I'm going to soak in the bath for a couple of hours.
Their land shall be soaked with blood.

senses.d: To immerse in liquid to the point of saturation or thorough permeation.
ex: Soak the beans overnight before cooking.

senses.d: To penetrate or permeate by saturation.
ex: The water soaked into my shoes and gave me wet feet.
The rivulet beneath […]soaked its way obscurely through wreaths of snow.

senses.d: To allow (especially a liquid) to be absorbed; to take in, receive. (usually + up)
ex: A sponge soaks up water; the skin soaks in moisture.
I soaked up all the knowledge I could at university.

senses.d: To overcharge or swindle out of a large amount of money.
To drink intemperately or gluttonously.
To heat (a metal) before shaping it.
To hold a kiln at a particular temperature for a given period of time.
ex: We should soak the kiln at cone 9 for half an hour.

senses.d: To absorb; to drain.
ex: That they will want a certaine sucking and soaking

senses.d: To engage in penetrative sex without hip thrusting.
(slang, boxing) To hit or strike.
ex: Wasn't Mr. Sipperley pretty shirty when he came to and found that you had been soaking him with putters?

senses.d: An immersion in water etc.
ex: After the strenuous climb, I had a nice long soak in a bath.

senses.d: A drunkard.
A carouse; a drinking session.
A low-lying depression that fills with water after rain.
ex: I set off early to walk along the Melbourne Road where, one of the punters had told me, there was a soak with plenty of frogs in it.
Molly and Daisy finished their breakfast and decided to take all their dirty clothes and wash them in the soak further down the river.
